strengths: Identifies and formalizes an important but overlooked problem in CIL evaluation (RS protocol's inadequacy)
Provides solid theoretical analysis with multiple theorems and proofs, including sample complexity reduction from O(N ln N/ε²) to O(R(σ)²)
Comprehensive experimental validation with ground-truth distributions on enumerable scenarios (90 sequences) using multiple datasets and methods
Practical and reproducible algorithm using CLIP embeddings with reasonable computational complexity
Clear motivation and presentation with compelling visualizations (Figure 1); thorough appendix with detailed proofs and supplementary experiments
Reveals actionable insights about CIL robustness (e.g., multiple methods converge to similar worst-case performance)
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: core idea of extreme sequence sampling is intuitive; combines standard techniques (clustering, greedy selection) without fundamental innovation
Critical evaluation limitation: experiments only on 90 sequences (6 classes) far from realistic CIL with 100-1000+ classes; scalability to realistic scenarios not validated

Strong dependency on CLIP without robust alternatives: no ablation studies for alternative similarity measures; performance varies with CLIP model choice; unclear effectiveness in domains where CLIP is weak

Theoretical gaps: Theorem 3's proof uses undefined proportionality constant α; connection between parameter distance and generalization error is informal (Equation 35); provides only directional guarantees without quantitative bounds
Unclear practical impact: better distribution estimates don't guarantee better model selection; no empirical evidence that EDGE-found extremes match true extremes; missing analysis of when EDGE fails

Questionable design choices: no justification for exactly 3 sequences (hard/easy/median); median sequence selection is arbitrary/random; using mean/variance of 3 samples inadequate; no confidence intervals on estimates
Missing statistical rigor: no significance tests on improvements; marginal gains for stable methods (e.g., Table 1 EASE); Gaussian distribution assumption fails for some methods (Table A3)
Limited evaluation scope: only vision classification; no experiments on full CIFAR-100 or larger realistic settings; restricted to similar domains

strengths: Identifies and rigorously addresses a genuine and under-appreciated flaw in standard CIL evaluation protocols
Solid theoretical foundation with formal sample complexity analysis (Theorems 1-2) showing extreme sequences reduce required samples from O(N ln N) to O((R(σ))²)
Comprehensive experimental validation including enumerable experiments with ground-truth 90-sequence distributions across multiple datasets and 20+ methods
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figure 1) demonstrating the practical impact of the problem
Practical implementation integrated with existing CIL toolboxes (PILOT, PyCIL) with minimal user friction
Extensive supplementary analysis including robustness to CLIP architectures (Figure 4) and comparison with alternative baselines (Appendix D.4)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty—core insight (sampling factorial space inadequately) is somewhat intuitive; solution relies on standard hierarchical clustering rather than novel optimization techniques

CLIP text embedding dependency creates domain applicability concerns: non-natural image domains show poor alignment (Appendix D.3.2: Spearman's ρ=0.279-0.588 for medical imaging without LLM augmentation), ~0.15 MAE deviation from image-based similarity

Incomplete justification of protocol design: no ablation on why exactly 3 sequences (hard/easy/median); 'median guaranteed near center' claim lacks formal proof; Algorithm 1's greedy approach optimality unanalyzed

Gap between theory and practice: Theorem 3 relies on strong overparameterization assumptions from Lin et al. (2023); Gaussian approximation validated post-hoc via Box-Cox transformation, which is circular

Limited guidance for practitioners: for ~30% of methods (EASE, MOS, RanPAC), RS and EDGE achieve equivalent performance (near-zero JSD/Wasserstein); paper doesn't clarify when CLIP overhead is justified vs. using 6 random samples
Scalability not demonstrated: O(|G|(N³ + K³)) complexity, experiments only on ≤100 classes; applicability to modern 1000+ class datasets unclear

Fairness of evaluation comparison: RS uses fixed seeds {0,42,1993} without justification; statistical significance testing absent despite n=3 sample sizes; wall-clock time comparison missing; Figure A6 shows RS needs only 5-6 samples to match EDGE in 90-sequence space

strengths: Identifies and formalizes an important but overlooked flaw in CIL evaluation protocols, with concrete evidence that random sampling produces systematically biased estimates

Provides strong theoretical foundation: Theorem 1 establishes prohibitive sample complexity for RS (O(N ln N/ε²)), while Theorem 2 shows extreme sequences reduce this to O((R(σ))²)—elegant justification for the approach
Comprehensive experimental validation including novel enumerable setting with 90 ground-truth sequences, normality testing, multiple datasets, and both pre-trained/non-pretrained methods
Practical algorithm that is computationally efficient (0.5-0.9s), implementable without image access using CLIP text embeddings, with code release promised
Excellent presentation with intuitive figures (particularly Figure 1) and clear narrative that makes the evaluation problem accessible; valuable insights about method convergence at lower bounds
Demonstrates consistent improvements: EDGE produces dramatically better distribution approximations (JSD and Wasserstein distances consistently lower than RS) and more reliable model rankings
weaknesses: Theorem 3 lacks sufficient rigor for a top-tier venue: makes unjustified assumptions about optimal parameters and parameter proportionality (Eq. 35) without formal proof; the connection between task similarity and generalization error needs more formal treatment

Critical CLIP dependency: Section D.3.2 reveals severe limitations for specialized domains (medical images show Spearman ρ=0.588 and 0.279, not significant); requires complex LLM augmentation with no clear fallback strategy when similarity-performance correlation breaks down

Incomplete characterization of when EDGE is beneficial: On stable methods (EASE, RanPAC), JSD=0 indicating RS and EDGE are equivalent; paper doesn't identify which algorithm/dataset combinations most benefit from EDGE or analyze failure modes
Only uses 3 sequences for EDGE (hard/easy/median) without ablation or justification; Appendix D.5 shows convergence to RS at 10-20 samples, raising questions about optimality of this choice

Limited scope of enumerable experiments: only 6 classes in 3 tasks (unrealistically small); ImageNet-R shows much smaller gaps than CIFAR-100; CUB-200 results less dramatic—unclear if findings scale to realistic 100+ class settings

Methodological concerns: Algorithm 1's multi-granularity clustering is under-motivated; Theorem 4 only provides probabilistic greedy optimality bounds with no practical guarantees; hierarchical clustering linkage choice not discussed; alternative similarity metrics not compared
Moderate novelty: core ideas (random sampling misses extremes, use similarity for sequence generation) are fairly straightforward; contribution is strong execution rather than conceptual innovation
